 1   II.             Overview

 2   Q.      What topics will you address in your testimony?

 3   A.      I address two principal subjects: first, the Company’s proposed Low-Income Rider (LIR),

 4           including affordability, cost recovery, eligibility, and reporting; and second, specific

 5           concerns with the Company’s streetlighting tariffs, including LED equivalencies, obsolete

 6           lighting technologies, conversion costs, and tariff design.

 7   Q.      How much is the Company proposing to raise its rates?

 8   A.      The Company is proposing an overall revenue increase of 50.4%, including an increase in

 9           residential rate revenue of 73.1%. (25-00082-UT, El Paso Electric Company’s Proposed

10           Notice to Customers, p3.)

11   Q.      How much of the proposed increases can be attributed to cumulative inflation since

12           the Company’s last general rate case?

13   A.      Cumulative actual and projected inflation from the effective date of the Company’s last

14           rate increase (20-00104, effective July 2021) to the beginning of the projected test year in

15           the instant case (January 1, 2027) is 22.7%, for a compound annual inflation rate of 3.8%1.




     1
      CPI-U in June 2021 was 273.003. Projected CPI-U for January 2027 is 335.0 (per Financial Forecast Center).
     Total change is 22.7%.

  1        The Company’s proposed overall total rate increase is 2.2x actual and projected inflation

 2        and the proposed increase to residential rates is 3.22x inflation.

 3   Q.   Why is it meaningful to compare changes in the Company’s rates and revenue to the

 4        rate of inflation?

 5   A.   There are two reasons to compare the Company’s rate growth to inflation.

 6        The first is to observe whether the Company is controlling its costs, and by extension its

 7        rates, effectively. A regulated monopoly utility does not face competitive market pressures

 8        that constrain its ability to mark up its prices to fully recover cost increases. Its customers

 9        cannot take their business elsewhere if they are dissatisfied with the utility’s prices or

10        service quality, nor can they easily, quickly or significantly change their consumption of

11        electricity in response to price signals. It is therefore up to the Commission to protect

12        customers by ensuring the Company’s costs are reasonable. Inflation is a useful and

13        relevant benchmark because it compares the Company’s rates to prices of a broad market-

14        basket of goods and services. If the Company’s rates rise faster than inflation, this is a

15        reasonable if not dispositive indicator that the Company is not controlling costs as well as

16        companies that operate in competitive markets. The Commission should consider whether

17        super-inflationary cost increases are justified by increases in sales, incremental legal and

18        regulatory costs or other justifying factors. Even if present, however, these factors do not

19        automatically relieve the Company of responsibility to manage its costs: for example, all

20        large companies must manage legal and regulatory costs and can no more freely mark up

21        their prices to recover them than they can any other kind of cost. If the Commission allows

22        the utility to recover 100% of its cost increases without such deep inquiry, then the



                                                    7
  1           company will have little incentive to control its costs by innovating and becoming more

 2           efficient and productive in the ways that companies operating in competitive markets must.

 3           The second reason to compare the utility’s costs to inflation is to advance energy

 4           affordability and security for customers. If rates rise faster than inflation, they are also

 5           likely to rise faster than household incomes and increase household energy burdens. In

 6           New Mexico, median household income increased only about 2.5% from 2021 through

 7           2024 (latest available figures), a figure far outstripped by the Company’s proposed 73%

 8           increase in residential rates.2 Therefore, in New Mexico, in recent years household income

 9           has not even kept up with inflation. Notwithstanding the consumer perspective, it is

10           reasonable for the Commission to evaluate the Company’s growth in costs using general

11           inflation as a comparison to other companies’ ability to control costs.

12           Comparing costs using inflation as a yardstick goes to prudence of the Company’s

13           expenditures, and comparing revenue increases to inflation goes to fairness to customers.

14           By either measure, the Company’s rate proposal demands very careful scrutiny.

15   Q.      Do you support the Company’s proposed low-income rider?

16   A.      Yes, I support the LIR but with changes. I support the credit because the Company’s

17           proposed residential rate increase will likely create financial hardship for low-income and

18           fixed-income customers and may also increase utility costs associated with arrears,

19           collection activity, and uncollectible accounts.

  1            I support provision of credits specifically that offset fixed charges for low-income

 2            customers because those charges are regressive, that is, fixed charges constitute a larger

 3            percentage of household income for low-income than for other households. Additionally,

 4            fixed charges provide no financial incentives for customers to change their energy use

 5            behaviors – customers cannot reduce them by using less electricity.

 6            My reservations arise from:


 7        •   The Company’s proposed direct assignment of the cost of the LIR to the residential rate

 8            class;

 9        •   The Company’s proposed use of SNAP beneficiary data to determine LIR eligibility, which

10            may be legally problematic and would very likely result in much higher program cost than

11            the Company projects;

12        •   Absence of any proposed reporting framework to help the Commission, Company and

13            stakeholders assess impact and effectiveness of the LIR.

14            I will explain each of my reservations in turn. First, I will explore the need for billpayer

15            assistance and the impact the proposed LIR is likely to have on that need.

16   Q.       How many residential customers need energy assistance?

17   A.       Energy assistance eligibility is commonly predicated on household income as a percentage

18            of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL), with 150% to 200% of FPL being common eligibility

19            caps. Thus, we can very conservatively estimate the level of energy assistance needed by

20            determining the number of households served by the Company that come in below 100%

21            of FPL.

 2        Community Survey (“ACS”), Dona Ana and Otero Counties have 111,811 households of

  1   Q.   Do you therefore recommend that the Commission increase the funds allocated to pay

 2        for the LIR?

 3   A.   No, I do not. I say this reluctantly, mindful that many low-income households would not

 4        promptly receive assistance they badly need and will need even more once EPE’s rates go

 5        up.

 6        Rather than expecting that the LIR might serve a majority of eligible households and make

 7        a significant dent in low-income energy burden, I recommend that the Commission and

 8        Company initially view the LIR as a pilot program, with the intention of learning how to

 9        deliver assistance efficiently and measure its impact. This approach is desirable because

10        energy assistance costs must be recovered from other ratepayers. It behooves all parties, in

11        that light, to learn how to run a cost-effective program before incurring larger costs to serve

12        all low-income customers. Otherwise, the increased burden of cost recovery on all

13        customers may overshadow the benefits to low-income customers.

14        As a pilot program, the LIR should not be evaluated by its success in reducing the overall

15        energy burden; it should be evaluated by its success in reducing the energy burden for the

16        customers it serves. The Company and Commission should be prepared to evaluate the LIR

17        after a suitable pilot period and decide how to extend its reach.

18   Q.   What changes do you recommend to the Company’s LIR credit proposal?

19   A.   I propose changes in how the cost of the credit is recovered, how the Company determines

20        eligibility and in reporting requirements. I describe each of these recommendations in turn

21        below.

22   Q.   How does the Company propose to recover the cost of the LIR?

                                                    12
  1   A.        The Company proposes to directly assign recovery of the LIR cost entirely to the residential

 2             class (Carrasco direct, p41, lines 8-19).

 3   Q.        Do you support the Company’s proposed allocation of LIR cost?

 4   A.        No, I do not. Allocation to the residential class is not consistent with cost causation and is

 5             not required under the enabling statute.

 6   Q.        Please describe relevant aspects of the statute enabling the Commission to adopt low-

 7             income rates.

 8   A.        In 2025, New Mexico enacted legislation (House Bill 91) authorizing the Commission to

 9             approve rates and programs designed to reduce the energy burden for low-income

10             customers, explicitly recognizing affordability as a legitimate ratemaking objective.

11   Q.        Does the statute specify cost recovery mechanisms?

12   A.        The statute authorizes programs and rates but does not prescribe a specific cost allocation

13             method, leaving the Commission discretion to apply traditional ratemaking principles.

14   Q.        Has the issue of cost shifting been recognized in New Mexico proceedings?

15   A.        Yes. Legislative and policy discussions surrounding HB 91 explicitly acknowledged that

16             when low-income customers cannot pay, the resulting costs are already borne by other

17             ratepayers, reinforcing the system-wide nature of affordability costs.4

18   Q.        Why would recovery of LIR cost entirely from the residential class not be consistent

19             with cost causation?

                                                            13
  1   A.   The LIR cost will be incurred in furtherance of a public policy objective stemming from

 2        the Company’s obligation to serve all customers and from the statute authorizing the

 3        Commission to approve low-income rates. EPE’s obligation to serve reflects a public policy

 4        requirement that the Company serve customers who may struggle to pay their bills. An

 5        unregulated company might simply refuse to serve a customer who cannot pay fully or

 6        consistently; the cost of EPE’s obligation to serve those customers is caused by a public

 7        policy choice.

 8        It follows that recovering costs of the LIR only within the residential class would force

 9        other, non-low-income residential customers to pay for a cost they do not cause: the fact

10        that some residential customers struggle to pay their bills should confer no responsibility

11        on better-off customers who happen to be in the same rate class. Again, the LIR cost is

12        caused by a public policy objective, not by the residential rate class. Thus, it is a general

13        cost of doing business that should be recovered from all customers.

14   Q.   How should LIR costs be classified for allocation purposes?

15   A.   LIR costs should be classified as joint and common costs:


16           •   They are not driven by marginal consumption or usage characteristics.

17           •   They arise from system-wide service obligations.

18           •   They support the integrity and financial viability of the utility system as a whole.

 2             administrative costs that cannot be directly assigned and must be allocated across all

 3             customer classes using appropriate allocators.5

 4   Q.        Will the LIR create benefits shared across customer classes?

 5   A.        Yes, it will create system-wide benefits. It will help to reduce uncollectible expense, lower

 6             disconnection and reconnection costs and improve revenue stability.

 7   Q.        Is EPE’s proposed direct assignment of LIR costs to the residential rate class

 8             consistent with how it allocates uncollectible expenses?

 9   A.        No. It is not, but it should be. EPE allocates uncollectible costs by revenue per customer

10             class, rather than allocating uncollectible costs proportional to uncollectibles generated

11             within each class. This allocation reflects the fact that any given residential customer is not

12             responsible for any other residential customer’s inability to pay their bill. The same

13             observation is true with respect to the LIR.

14   Q.        What rate design do you recommend for recovery of LIR credit costs?

15   A.        Because the proposed Low-Income Rider is intended to advance a broad public-policy

16             objective rather than recover costs directly caused by any particular customer class,

17             recovery through a uniform volumetric charge across all customer classes is reasonable.

18             This approach follows the same rationale and approach as recovery of uncollectible costs.

19             A volumetric charge ensures that customers consuming greater amounts of electricity,

20             including large commercial and industrial customers, contribute proportionately more

21             toward funding the program. By contrast, a fixed surcharge would require largely arbitrary

 8   Q.   What changes do you propose to the Company’s proposed method for determining

 9        eligibility to receive the LIR credit?

10   A.   I recommend that the Company use only LIHEAP participation to determine eligibility for

11        the LIR credit at the pilot stage. I make this recommendation because the Company’s

12        proposal to use SNAP data may be legally problematic and would likely expand

13        participation and program cost substantially. I am not opposed to broader assistance in the

14        longer term, but the Company should first establish a legally sound, administratively

15        workable, and measurable pilot program.

16   Q.   Why might the Company’s plans to use SNAP eligibility to identify LIR recipients

17        prove to be legally problematic?

18   A.   The Company has not explained why it believes it will be able to access SNAP data for

19        LIR determination purposes.

20        SNAP recipient data were gathered for the purpose of providing food aid. Federal benefit

21        programs may limit use and disclosure of personal information to program purposes, and

22        the Company has not stated how energy assistance eligibility determination is consistent

 2           personal data sharing it describes. The state recently refused a federal request for SNAP

 4           is reluctant to share SNAP data even with the federal government, it will likely scrutinize

 5           (or prohibit) sharing with a utility even more strictly.

 6           This concern is also significant from the perspective of a SNAP recipient. People who

 7           receive food assistance have a reasonable expectation of privacy. Disclosing to an electric

10           Because of this concern, and because inclusion of SNAP participants seems likely to

15           customer data privacy.

 4        simple fairness and to make the tariff easier for customers to understand. When the day

 5        comes that the Company is forced to convert an HPS luminaire to LED because

 6        replacement lamps are unavailable on the market, that customer thereafter enjoys not only

 7        a lower LED rate but also better lighting purely by happenstance of when their lamp burned

 8        out. That customer’s neighbor, whose HPS lamp burned out only a week earlier and was

 9        re-lamped with one of the last HPS lamps the Company had in stock, would pay a higher

10        HPS rate for the life of the new lamp (typically six years) purely because their HPS lamp

11        burned out just a bit sooner. The difference in timing is beyond the customers’ control.

12        Therefore they do not cause the difference in cost, and they should not pay a different tariff.

13        A unified tariff would simply charge customers the same tariff for equivalent lighting

14        regardless of what kind of luminaire they have. If it were judged that a 100w HPS and a

15        31w LED were equivalent, as the Company now represents, and the customer does not

16        control the decision of when their HPS light gets converted, then they are not causing the

17        difference in cost of service and they should pay the same tariff. That tariff can be

18        determined as a levelized average cost of all luminaire types that deliver the same level of

19        illumination. It is true that functionally equivalent LED and HID luminaires cause different

20        costs; my point here is customers do not cause that difference when they no longer have a

21        choice what kind of luminaire they have, and the moment when their luminaire is converted

22        to LED is purely a matter of chance.

     1 Introduction

The DesignLights Consortium (DLC) is a nonprofit organization committed to accelerating the transition
to energy efficient lighting and controls. Through rigorous qualification programs and stakeholder
engagement, the DLC supports policies and programs that reduce energy use, carbon emissions, and
light pollution, and that ultimately promote quality lighting and a more sustainable world. The DLC’s
work is enabled by stakeholder collaboration, which includes manufacturers, efficiency program
administrators, and users of the QPLs who support the continued evolution of high-performing, energy
efficient, non-residential1 LED lighting solutions. Over the past 10 years, the LED revolution and
manufacturer innovation has helped enable energy efficiency programs to achieve over 1,000 terawatt-
hours (TWh) of lighting energy savings.

Released in 2020, SSL Version 5.1 marked the last major update to DLC’s SSL requirements, emphasizing
quality of light and controllability. Over the past 5 years, the DLC has engaged deeply with industry
partners, including serving on standards development committees, conducting outreach, and developing
studies that advance LED retrofits, energy efficient controls, and reduced light pollution.

Building on that foundation, the DLC Technical Requirements for LED Lighting: SSL V6.0 & LUNA V2.0
unites previously separate documents into one streamlined set of qualification criteria for the Solid-
State Lighting and LUNA Qualified Products Lists. Like all DLC updates, these requirements were shaped
through extensive stakeholder input, including years of collaboration, a 2024 call for feedback, and two
rounds of public comment.

where it matters to drive lasting impact. By setting clear, credible performance baselines, SSL V6.0 and

2.2 Eligibility Guidance for the "Specialty" Primary Use Designation
Products with a Specialty designation are not eligible for DLC Premium qualification. The same model
number cannot be used for both a specialty and a non-specialty product.

Principles for evaluating products submitted with the Specialty designation:
1. Products must meet the intended use of the broader category and general application group under
   which they are designated. For example, products seeking qualification with a designation of
   Outdoor Low Output-Specialty: _____ must be intended for use in outdoor applications.
2. Products must meet the minimum performance requirements of the broader category under which
   they are designated.
3. Products must report distribution data but are not required to meet specific distribution criteria.
4. Products must specify the end use for which they are intended. For example, products that are
   intended to be used for canopy lighting that seek qualification under the Specialty designation must
   indicate on the application form that their intended use is "Specialty: Canopy Lighting". DLC staff
   monitor terminology and may make minor modifications to descriptor terms to ensure consistency
   (for example, "Specialty: Canopy Lighting” vs. "Specialty: Canopy Luminaire"). Changes to descriptor
   terms will be made in consultation with the applicant.
5. As part of the evaluation of any new Specialty designation, the DLC will determine what dimming
   requirements apply to that designation. Additional details on the application and market for the
   end-use may be requested.
6. The DLC retains the right to deny the Specialty designation for any product that it does not believe
   meets the intended use of the designation. Judgment on eligibility will be at the sole discretion of
   the DLC program staff.


2.3 Eligibility for Hazardous Environment Products
Manufacturers submitting products labeled as suitable for hazardous environments must provide
documentation that supports those claims. This documentation must clearly indicate that the model
numbers in question are certified to the UL 844 standard and specify the Class and Division for which the
products are certified. In cases where questions arise, the DLC will require that the documentation from
the relevant safety organization explicitly identifies both the model numbers and the certification to the
UL 844 standard.

4.1 Introduction
The term “quality of light” encompasses the characteristics of lighting that include spectrum,
distribution, and color maintenance, as well as application considerations such as uniformity, discomfort
from glare, light trespass, and light pollution. DLC Standard quality of light requirements ensure basic
quality of light performance for all listed products. Under this version of the technical requirements, a
product’s quality of light is evaluated by its spectral quality, light output, and distribution, with
additional considerations for discomfort from glare for the DLC Premium qualification. Additionally, this
version of the technical requirements sets lower CCT thresholds for Outdoor PUDs, clarifies
requirements for linear replacement lamps and omnidirectional and directional E26 and E39 lamps, and
introduces optional reporting of ANSI/IES TM-35-19 CS4 and CS7 values.

4.3.2.1 BUG (Backlight, Uplight, and Glare) Ratings
SSL products in the Outdoor Luminaire and Retrofit Kits categories shall report the six-character BUG
ratings. The nomenclature of BUG Ratings is similar to this example: B2-U0-G2.
In addition, for products tested for distribution, tested BUG ratings will be generated by the DLC
reviewer using the photometric data (IES-format file) and listed under the Tested Data section of the
QPL.
Applicability to future Specialty Primary Use Designations will be determined on a case-by-case basis.
The following Outdoor Low, Mid, High, or Very High Output PUDs are exempt from SSL V6.0 BUG rating
reporting requirements:
    •     Architectural Flood and Spot Luminaires
    •     Specialty: Wall Grazing/Slicing
    •     Specialty: Hazardous Environment Flood and Spot Luminaires
    •     Specialty: Soffit Lighting
    •     Specialty: Natatorium Lighting
    •     Specialty: Tunnel Lighting
    •     Sports Lighting

    •     Lamp PUDs do not need to report BUG Ratings

4.4 Interactions With Other DLC Policies: Field Adjustable Light
    Distribution (FALD) and Field Adjustable Light Output (FALO)
For FALD products, additional clarifications on meeting light distribution and discomfort glare
requirements are as follows:
    •   Testing and reporting requirements for zonal lumen distributions (ZLD) and spacing criteria (SC)
        are applicable to FALD products. The DLC review process will verify the ZLD requirements per
        the ZLD and SC measurements at the light distribution setting designated by the manufacturer
        per the Field Adjustable Light Distribution (FALD) Testing and Reporting Requirements.
    •   Testing and reporting requirements for BUG ratings are applicable to FALD products in the
        Outdoor Luminaire and Retrofit Kit categories, except for the PUDs that are exempted from
        reporting BUG Ratings (see BUG (Backlight, Uplight, and Glare) Ratings). This data will be
        displayed in the product detail page of the SSL QPL.
            o    Tested BUG ratings will be listed on the SSL QPL under the Tested Data section.
            o    Reported BUG ratings will be listed on the SSL QPL under the Reported Data section.
    •   Testing and reporting requirements for Unified Glare Rating (UGR) are applicable to FALD
        products in the applicable categories seeking Premium qualification. The UGR values shall meet
        the threshold at the light distribution setting designated, per the FALD Testing and Reporting
        Requirements, for meeting the ZLD requirements of the PUD, for which product qualification is
        sought.
    •   Testing and reporting requirements for UGR are applicable to FALD products for which efficacy
        allowances are sought. FALD products are eligible for efficacy allowances related to UGR under
        V6.0.

For FALO products, the minimum light output thresholds provided in Light Output and Distribution
Requirements apply to the products at their maximum FALO setting (maximum wattage), and not at
lower settings.

5.1 Introduction
To better support expansion of energy efficiency incentive programs for luminaires with integral
controls and controls-ready luminaires, SSL V6.0 and LUNA V2.0 add Controls Categories to associate
products with specific integral controls options. Controls Categories are designed to align with energy
savings claims associated with specific lighting control strategies, which are detailed in various Technical
Resource Manuals (TRMs) and efficiency program policies. As TRMs govern many energy efficiency
programs3, Controls Categories will simplify incentive program application and review processes and
lower barriers to the adoption of advanced lighting by directly connecting model number variations of
products with integral controls to lighting control strategies and their associated energy savings factors.
